PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:26 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11409-1 A comprehensive review of current robot-based pollinators for crop pollination Rajmeet Singh1 · Lakmal Seneviratne1 · Irfan Hussain1 Received: 25 March 2024 / Accepted: 23 September 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract The decline of bee and wind-based pollination systems in greenhouses due to controlled environments and limited access has boosted the importance of finding alternative pol- lination methods. Robot-based pollination systems have emerged as a promising solution, ensuring adequate crop yield even in challenging pollination scenarios. This paper pres- ents a comprehensive review of the current robotic-based pollinators employed in agricul- ture. The review categorizes pollinator technologies into major categories such as air-jet, water-jet, linear actuator, ultrasonic wave, and air-liquid spray, each suitable for specific crop pollination requirements. However, these technologies are often tailored to particular crops, limiting their versatility. The advancement of science and technology has led to the integration of automated pollination technology, encompassing information technol- ogy, automatic perception, detection, control, and operation. This integration not only re- duces labor shortage problem but also fosters the ongoing progress of modern agriculture by refining technology, enhancing automation, and promoting intelligence in agricultural practices. Finally, the challenges encountered in the design of robot-based pollinators are addressed, and a forward-looking perspective is taken towards future developments, aim- ing to contribute to the sustainable advancement of this technology. Singh et al. 1 Introduction The agricultural sector is currently struggling with pollination deficits related to the decreases of natural pollinators (Potts et al. 2016) i.e. wild pollinators and labor shortage issue (Hertz and Zahniser 2013) which constitute a significant threat for crop production. This concern is particularly pronounced within the context of greenhouse farming, where many farmers are unable to depend solely on the presence of natural pollinators within their controlled environments for efficient crop pollination. The cultivation of pollinator-dependent crops is expanding worldwide, resulting in a greater reliance on bees and their pollination services (Aizen et al. 2008, 2019). Despite efforts to increase the bee colonies count globally, the growth rate has been insufficient to meet the rising demand (Mashilingi et al. 2022). Conse- quently, this supply–demand disparity has led to pollination deficits (Reilly et al. 2020) and a subsequent surge in prices for pollination services (Rucker et al. 2012). Figure 1 depicts the agriculture dependence on pollinators as per Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) dataset (Potts et al. 2016). Greenhouse farming has become an essential component of modern agriculture, enabling controlled and efficient cultivation of crops. However, the diminishing population of natural pollinators, including bees, presents a notable challenge to achieving effective pollination within greenhouse environments. Figure 2 mentioned the annual growth rate (percentage per year) in the number of honeybee hives (Potts et al. 2016). This challenge has prompted the exploration of innovative solutions, including robot- based pollination, to ensure efficient and reliable pollination in greenhouse farming (House 2014). There are several reasons why bees are less prevalent in greenhouses compared to outdoor agriculture environments: ● Limited access: Greenhouses are enclosed structures designed to create a controlled environment for plant growth. The access points for bees to enter and exit may be re- Fig. 1 World map showing agriculture dependence on pollinators (i.e., the percentage of expected agri- culture production volume loss in the absence of pollination) in 1961 and 2012, based on FAO dataset (FAOSTAT 2013) 1 3 A comprehensive review of current robot-based pollinators for crop… Page 3 of 29 26 Fig. 2 World map showing the annual growth rate in the number of honeybee hives from countries report- ing those data to FAO between 1961 and 2012 (FAOSTAT 2013) stricted, making it difficult for them to access the greenhouse and carry out pollination effectively. ● Altered floral landscape: Greenhouse crops often consist of specific plant species that are selected for their productivity and suitability for controlled environments. This may result in a limited variety of flowers compared to natural habitats, reducing the attrac- tiveness of the greenhouse for bees. ● Pesticide use: Greenhouses typically employ intensive pest management strategies to protect crops from pests and diseases. The use of pesticides and other chemical treat- ments may accidentally harm bees and deter them from entering the greenhouse. ● Temperature and humidity: Greenhouses provide a controlled climate with specific temperature and humidity conditions optimized for plant growth. These conditions may not be ideal for bees, which prefer a more natural outdoor environment. As a result, alternative pollination methods are often employed to ensure successful crop pollination in these controlled environments. Robot-based pollination is emerging as a promising technique among the potential alternatives. Recently, there has been extensive research conducted on the integration of robots in the field of agriculture. Numerous notable applications include the automated harvesting of crops (Sarig 1993; Henten et al. 2002; Baeten et al. 2008; Scarfe et al. 2009; Lehnert et al. 2017; Lochan et al. 2024), the identification and removal of weeds (Lee et al. 1999; Blasco et al. 2002; Åstrand et al. 2002; Slaughter et al. 2008), as well as the mapping, dataset collec- tion, and phenotyping (Weiss et al. 2011; Cheein et al. 2011; Peña et al. 2013; Mueller-Sim et al. 2017). These advancements exemplify how robots add in to the concept of “precision agriculture”, wherein crop datasets are utilized to make informed decisions regarding sus- tainable and tailored crop cultivation and maintenance practices (Bongiovanni et al. 2004; McBratney et al. 2005; Zhang et al. 2012). In addition to their role in data gathering, robots can significantly enhance precision agriculture by executing individualized treatments and maintenance tasks. While humans may be capable of performing these tasks manually in 1 3 26 Page 4 of 29 R. Singh et al. small-scale productions, the use of robots holds great promise for large farms, where they can potentially offer increased efficiency and cost-effectiveness in the long run. In recent years, the concept of employing robots as pollinators has gained traction as a response to the decline in bee populations (Binns 2009; Potts et al. 2016). The precise task of pollinating a significant number of flowers is ideally suited for robots. When we hear the term “robot- based pollination”, it often evokes picture of tiny, bee-like design buzzing around flowers. Researchers have been focusing on the development of tiny, bee-like flying robots (Wood 2008; Ma et al. 2013) and exploring control strategies for managing swarms of these minia- ture flyers. The ultimate goal of such research is to enable these robots to contribute to crop pollination (Berman et al. 2011). Although these early-stage demonstrations showcase the potential viability of robot-based pollination, there are significant challenges that need to be addressed for flying robot-based approaches. These challenges include ensuring autonomy, extending the duration of flight, ensuring safety, and mitigating the impact of wind distur- bances on the flowers (Wood et al. 2013). Artificial intelligence and Machine learning plays a vital role in agriculture (Padhiary et al. 2025). Automation and AI in the precision agricul- ture for enhancing the crop management system (Hoque et al. 2024; Padhiary et al. 2024). Ground-based robotic pollination systems have been explored through various examples. These include a fixed crane like structure used for pollinating vanilla plants (Shaneyfelt et al. 2013), a mobile robotic arm design intended for tall tree pollination (Gan-Mor et al. 2008), and a mobile robot platform specifically designed for pollinating tomato plants (Yuan et al. 2016). However, research in the field of ground-based mobile robotic pollination sys- tems is currently limited, with only a few examples and conceptual designs available. More- over, significant autonomy in these systems has yet to be demonstrated. This review was conducted using a targeted search approach and bibliometric analysis tools. The research focused on specific keywords such as “pollination,” “pollinator,” and “pollinator decline”. Thorough screening was performed to meticulously evaluate the rel- evance of papers, specifically considering their applicability to greenhouse agricultural con- texts. Papers that did not address pollination within the context of greenhouse agriculture were excluded, resulting in a final set of 585 papers that formed the basis of our analysis. Section 6 pro- vides a concluding summary of the paper. 2 Pollinators in tomato farming Tomato is a widely cultivated vegetable, occupying the top position in global crop produc- tion (Dingley et al. 2022). As per Dingley et al. (2022) the world wide annual production of tomato’s were 189.1 million tons, strawberries (9.2 million tons), and kiwifruits (4.4 million tons) in 2021. Despite its popularity, tomatoes, strawberries, and kiwifruits face various cultivation challenges, including the critical issue of pollination in greenhouses. Pollina- tion is the biological process in which pollen is transferred from the anthers to stigma, ultimately resulting in the formation of seeds and fruits. While some plant species require cross-pollination, tomatoes are self-pollinated once the pollen of a flower falls on the stigma of the same flower. The required movement of the pollen from the anthers to the stigma is naturally facilitated by wind or insects. In greenhouse cultivation of tomatoes, three common methods are employed for pollina- tion. These methods include insect pollination, artificial pollination through manual flower vibration, and hormonal pollination using plant growth regulators. Maintaining and manag- ing insects for pollination can be challenging, especially considering their decreased activity in high temperatures during the summer (Dag 2008), which results in reduced pollination efficiency. Additionally, the use of commercial bumblebees is limited in countries like Japan and Australia due to concerns about ecological risks (Dingley et al. 2022; Nishimura 2021). Figure 8 shows the Tomato flower pollination overview process (a) Tomato flower structure, (b) Bee pollination, (c) Hand brush pollination, and (d) Vibrator toothbrush pollination. Insect-mediated pollination aligns with is a natural process where tomato flowers are pollinated through the shaking action of the flower when honeybees and bumblebees or other buzz pollinating insects gather pollen. However, managing and raising insects for pollination can be challenging and the effectiveness of pollination decreases when bees become inactive in high temperatures (Dag 2008). As a result, artificial pollination is often employed, involving manual flower vibration. In this process, farm workers visually iden- tify the mature flowers for pollination based on their appearance and use a vibrating instru- ment to shake them. These designs aim to address the pollination needs of different crops, considering both self-pollination and cross-pollination require- ments. Yuan et al. (2016) designed a pollinator for tomato farming in greenhouses, utiliz- ing a water-jet nozzle controlled by a solenoid valve. The pollinator, mounted on a mobile platform with a 6-degree-of-freedom robotic arm, offers precise control but can be complex due to multiple components. Shimizu and Sato (2018) proposed an ultrasonic wave-based pollination system for self-pollination in greenhouse strawberry farming. However, this sys- tem is not suitable for cross-pollination crops like kiwifruit and dates. Strader et al. (2019) developed a hand-in-eye pollinator for bramble plants, employing three linear actuators to vibrate the tip with a cotton bud for accurate and precise pollination. Williams et al. (2020) proposed a water jet spraying-based pollinator for kiwifruit farming, activating specific noz- zles based on a camera’s image analysis. However, camera blurriness is a drawback due to its parallel installation with the nozzle setup. Hao et al. (2023) and Li et al. (2022) improved the kiwifruit pollination design using a single water jet nozzle mounted on a 6-degree-of- freedom robotic arm, employing articulated and parallelogram mechanism-based manipu- lators for better flexibility. Researchers have also explored drone and air/water jet-based pollination systems for date palm farming (Alkhamis 2022; Gadiel 2020; Tech 2022). While autonomous navigation is still in development, skilled operators currently operate the drone for pollination. Arugga (2022) presented a commercial prototype of a multi-air jet-based pollinator for self-pollinating tomato farming in greenhouses. Hiraguri et al. (2023a) devel- oped a drone-based pollinator for tomato farming, but stability issues were encountered during vibrator operation. Ahmad et al. (2024) proposed a linear actuator-based pollinator design for watermelon farming, incorporating a 3D camera and a pollinator device mounted on a 6-degree-of-freedom robotic arm. However, pose estimation calculation inaccuracies between the camera and pollinator axes were addressed with a pose estimation correction algorithm, adding complexity to the system. Masuda et al. (2024) introduced a pneumatic- based pollinator design for self-pollinating tomato farming, featuring a flexible soft tube and 1 3 A comprehensive review of current robot-based pollinators for crop… Page 23 of 29 26 obstacle-free path generation capability. This pollinator, mounted on a two-degree-of-free- dom Cartesian system, combines tip vibration and pneumatic air blow for effective pollina- tion. To drive future advancements in crop pollination equipment, research and development should prioritize the development of simplified structures, enhanced pollination efficiency, and reduced manufacturing costs. Current equipment utilizes various technologies such as 3D camera, linear actuators, vibrators, ultrasonic waves, air jets, water jets, and drone spray- ers for the pollination process. The market for robot-based pollination is still in its early growth stages, but it holds significant potential, particularly in greenhouse environments. The trend for future pollination robots is to reduce research and development costs while improving the supporting infrastructure of pollination equipment to achieve cost-effective- ness. To create intelligent, efficient, versatile, and affordable pollinators, operators should monitor the real-time operational status of each facility and optimize parameters through experimentation. Furthermore, future developments should prioritize general-purpose func- tionality, intelligence, and user-friendliness to fully replace manual pollination and address the bee decline issue in greenhouse farming. Currently, the development and adoption of intelligent pollinators are progressing rapidly, leading to cost reductions and improved effi- ciency. This trend aligns with the future direction of intelligent general-purpose pollinators. Non-contact image sensors have emerged as a crucial factor in shaping the future of pol- linator design. As we look ahead, the integration of image sensors with diverse pollination technologies adds versatility and efficiency to the pollination process across different crop types in greenhouses.These advancements are driving the acceleration of the pollination process while simultaneously addressing cost-effectiveness. 6 Conclusion This paper reviews the progress of the application of pollinator design technology in the field of crop pollination. The paper explains various technologies used for pollinator design according to type of the crops. In this paper, self-pollination and cross-pollination crops are considered i.e. tomato, strawberry, kiwifruit, watermelon, date palm, bramble plants. robot-based pollination has emerged as a crucial solution to supplement insect pollinators in various cropping systems. Greenhouses, with their controlled environmental conditions, pose challenges for bee survival, making robotic pollinators essential. The development of different technologies, including air-jet, water-jet, ultrasonic wave, linear actuators, and air- liquid spray, has enabled artificial pollination. Each technology has its own advantages and drawbacks, and careful consideration is needed to select the most suitable approach for spe- cific crop requirements. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of artificial pollinator equipment, categorizing them based on technology, crop, develop- ment phase and identified drawbacks or gaps. This analysis helps identify areas where fur- ther research and improvement are needed to enhance pollination efficiency. With the rapid expansion of greenhouse crop plantations and rising labor costs, there is an urgent need for innovative robotic technologies to address the challenges of pollination. JSON: Name: multimodal_closedloop_pollinator Title: Multimodal closed-loop robotic pollination using fused vision, airflow and pollen sensing to improve greenhouse crop pollination outcomes Short Hypothesis: A multimodal closed-loop robotic pollinator that adaptively adjusts actuation parameters (air pressure, vibration amplitude, and nozzle activation) using fused RGB-D, airflow and pollen-detection feedback will increase flower-to-fruit set rate by at least 15 percentage points and reduce pollen consumption per flower by at least 30% compared to the best-performing open-loop baseline on greenhouse-grown tomato and kiwifruit under controlled conditions. Related Work: Existing robotic pollination approaches fall into several categories: open-loop air-jet or water-jet manifolds, vibration-based end-effectors, ultrasonic-actuated systems, solenoid/servo tip manipulators, and drone-mounted sprayers. Commercial deployments mainly use multiple air-jets for self-pollinating tomato rows; research prototypes use vibration tips for tomato and sprayed pollen suspension or single-nozzle manipulators for kiwifruit. Limitations across methods include crop-specific designs (self- versus cross-pollinators), open-loop actuation with no direct pollen-transfer sensing, camera blur or occlusion when actuators and optics are co-located, poor pollen metering leading to waste or insufficient transfer, limited workspace or reach for target flowers, high energy/payload constraints for airborne solutions, and scarce demonstrations of closed-loop adaptive control. No current system combines multisensor feedback (vision + flow + direct pollen sensing) with adaptive actuation to optimize both transfer efficiency and minimal crop damage across self- and cross-pollinating greenhouse crops. Abstract: Greenhouse crop production increasingly requires alternatives to insect pollinators due to limited bee access and labor constraints. Current robotic pollination systems are often crop-specific and operate open-loop, causing suboptimal pollen transfer, unnecessary pollen waste, and frequent crop contact damage. We propose a multimodal closed-loop robotic pollination pipeline that fuses RGB-D vision, local airflow measurement, and direct pollen-detection feedback to adaptively control actuation parameters including air pressure, vibration amplitude, and nozzle sequencing. The main contribution is an end-to-end sensor-fusion control architecture that jointly optimizes targeting accuracy, pollen dosage, and actuation profile for both self-pollinating (tomato) and cross-pollinating (kiwifruit) greenhouse crops. We evaluate the system in benchtop repeatability trials and randomized greenhouse experiments against representative open-loop and state-of-the-art baselines. Expected outcomes include statistically significant improvements in flower-to-fruit set rates, reductions in pollen consumption per flower, higher targeting precision, and measurable decreases in flower damage. The pipeline enables measurable, generalizable performance gains for robotic pollination across crop classes without reliance on pollinator insects. Experiments: Datasets and trials: 1) Benchtop synthetic-flower dataset: 1000 automated trials using instrumented artificial flowers with repeatable pollen-release models for parameter sweeps. 2) Greenhouse crop trials: two target crops—tomato (self-pollinating) and kiwifruit (cross-pollinating). For each crop perform randomized-block experiments with four conditions: (A) multimodal closed-loop system (proposed), (B) vision-only closed-loop (adaptive targeting but no pollen/flow feedback), (C) open-loop vibration/air-jet baseline tuned empirically, (D) best available commercial system baseline (air-jet manifold for tomato; single-nozzle spray manipulator for kiwifruit). Sample size: n=120 distinct flowers per condition per crop (480 flowers per crop, 960 total); additional replication across 3 greenhouse batches (total 2880 flowers). Evaluation metrics: flower-to-fruit set rate (%), pollen consumption per flower (mg), targeting accuracy (Euclidean error between nozzle/tip and flower center in mm), time per flower (s), flower damage rate (%), energy per flower (J). Experimental setup: mobile gantry or stationary gantry with 6-DOF manipulator, RGB-D camera and high-speed color camera, micro-anemometer at end-effector, optical particle counter or optical pollen sensor at nozzle/tip, end-effector force/vibration sensor. Control: closed-loop controller fusing vision, flow and pollen-detection to adapt air pressure (0–50 kPa), vibration frequency/amplitude (20–300 Hz), and nozzle pulse width. Data collection: log sensor streams, actuator commands, and outcome labels; follow-up fruit set measured at harvest window (crop-specific). Baselines and ablations: compare full multimodal closed-loop (A) vs (B) vision-only closed-loop vs (C) open-loop vs (D) commercial; ablation study within (A) removing pollen sensor, removing flow sensor, and removing force feedback (each ablation n=80 flowers). Analysis: perform ANOVA across conditions and post-hoc pairwise tests (Tukey) with significance threshold p<0.05, compute effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals; report per-crop and pooled results. Reproducibility: provide parameter logs and anonymized sensor traces for all trials. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sensor reliability and calibration drift (RGB-D depth errors, pollen sensor false positives/negatives); optical occlusion and camera blur caused by actuator motion or foliage; pollen sensor sensitivity to environmental humidity and particle contaminants; latency in sensor processing and control loop leading to mistimed actuation; limited generalization from greenhouse-controlled trials to open-field conditions; differences in pollen morphology across cultivars affecting transfer efficiency; potential flower damage from actuation if adaptive controller misestimates safe force or pressure; scalability constraints: per-flower time and energy may not meet commercial throughput requirements; hardware wear and maintenance needs for pollen-handling components; biosecurity and cross-contamination risk in shared pollen delivery systems; dataset and experimental bias toward greenhouse conditions, specific cultivars and environmental ranges (temperature/humidity), limiting external validity.
